title: Consent comes first
body: Everything in kink rests on consent: clear, enthusiastic, informed and revocable. Anyone can pause or stop at any time, for any reason, and doesn't owe an explanation. Pressure, guilt or being impaired by alcohol or drugs means there is no real consent.

title: Talk before you play
body: Before trying anything, talk about what you each want, what is off-limits, any health concerns, and what you'd like afterwards. A Yes/No/Maybe list can make this easier. Revisit the conversation as your interests change.

title: Agree on a way to stop
body: Pick a safeword, or use green, yellow and red, before anything begins. If someone can't speak, agree on a physical signal, like dropping an object. Stopping the moment someone uses the word is non-negotiable.

title: Start small and learn
body: Begin with low-intensity activities, and learn about anything with real physical risk from reliable sources, workshops or experienced mentors before trying it. Skills build over time, and nobody is expected to know everything at the start.

title: Keep safety gear close
body: If you try restraints, keep safety scissors within reach and never leave a restrained person alone. Pay attention to circulation, breathing and how your partner looks and sounds.

title: Avoid mixing with substances
body: Alcohol and drugs affect judgment, pain perception and the ability to consent. Many communities treat play under the influence as a serious breach of trust.

title: Care afterwards
body: Check in after play, and again in the following days. Emotional lows can follow intense scenes. Water, food, warmth and conversation help, and so can contacting a friend or counselor if you're struggling.

title: Trust your instincts
body: If someone ignores your limits, rushes you, or makes you feel uncomfortable, it is okay to leave. Good partners and communities welcome questions and respect 'no'. If you've been harmed, support organizations and a medical professional can help.
